(CNN) -- The mother and brother of a 31-year-old woman found strangled with her two young sons in the bedrooms of their home filed a wrongful death lawsuit Tuesday against the alleged killer -- the husband and father of the victims. Christopher Coleman has pleaded not guilty and is being held without bond. Christopher Coleman has pleaded not guilty in the triple homicide police say took place early in the morning on May 5 in the family home in the small southwestern Illinois city of Columbia. "To strip the culpable party of all financial holdings -- all that he has now and all that he may ever have," is the aim of the suit, said a statement accompanying the suit filed in Monroe County circuit court by Angela DeCicco and Mario Weiss, the mother and brother of Sheri Coleman. "To allow one penny of ill-gotten gain to be derived at the expense of Sheri, Garett and Gavin is not acceptable to those who dearly love them." The money would go to a memorial fund set up for Coleman and her sons, Garett, 11, and Gavin, 9 and "these funds will be used to erect a lasting tribute in the city of Columbia," according to the complaint. "Our goal is to extract something positive from such a horrific and senseless tragedy and to honor the lives of my sister and her two young sons," Weiss said. The wrongful death suit also names Coleman's father, Ronald, and the Joyce Meyer Ministries, where Coleman worked until shortly after his family was killed, as "respondents in discovery," which means they may be forced to hand over financial documents and information such as Coleman's personnel file, his work schedule and travel itineraries and the Ministries' employment policies. In addition, the suit tries to establish a timeline of events before and after the killings, saying the Colemans took the deed to their home in 2005, but six months ago, ownership was transferred to Christoper Coleman alone. "Sheri did not voluntarily sign the deed transferring title to the residence to Christopher," the document says. Lawyers in the civil suit also allege that in the period between the killings and his arrest, Coleman removed personal property from the home. The suit asks that Coleman and anyone "acting at his direction" be forbidden from entering the home again and that he provide a list of items already removed. Coleman remains in jail after a judge denied bond.

**Mother, brother of slain Illinois woman file wrongful death suit against husband**

**COLUMBIA, Illinois** — The mother and brother of Sheri Coleman, the Illinois woman found strangled alongside her two young sons in their family home, have filed a wrongful death lawsuit against her husband, Christopher Coleman.

The civil suit was filed after the May 2009 killings of Sheri Coleman, 31, and the couple’s sons, Garett, 11, and Gavin, 9, in Columbia, a small community southeast of St. Louis. Authorities said all three victims were found dead in their beds, and threatening messages had been spray-painted inside the home.

Christopher Coleman, who worked security for Joyce Meyer Ministries, initially told investigators he had received threats connected to his job. Prosecutors later alleged the threats were staged and that Coleman killed his family as his personal life unraveled.

The lawsuit, brought by members of Sheri Coleman’s family, seeks damages in connection with her death and the deaths of the children. Wrongful death claims are civil actions, separate from criminal prosecution, and can allow surviving relatives to pursue financial damages for the loss of loved ones.

Coleman was later convicted of murdering Sheri, Garett and Gavin Coleman and sentenced to life in prison without parole. He has maintained his innocence.

The murders shocked Columbia and drew national attention because of the brutality of the crime and the apparent attempt to make the killings appear tied to outside threats. Investigators said the evidence ultimately pointed back to Coleman, including inconsistencies in his account and details surrounding the threatening messages.

Sheri Coleman’s family has said publicly that their focus remains on seeking accountability and preserving the memory of Sheri and her sons.

## Wrongful death suit over Coleman family murders put spotlight on Joyce Meyer Ministries

**MONROE COUNTY, Illinois** — The murders of Sheri Coleman and her two young sons, Garett and Gavin, shocked the quiet community of Columbia, Illinois, and drew national attention not only because of the brutality of the crime, but because of the man convicted of carrying it out: Christopher Coleman, Sheri’s husband and the boys’ father, who worked in security for Joyce Meyer Ministries.

The case later moved beyond the criminal courtroom and into civil litigation, where relatives of the victims pursued a wrongful death suit in Monroe County. The lawsuit raised a haunting question: whether warning signs before the killings were mishandled, and whether Joyce Meyer Ministries bore any legal responsibility for what happened inside the Coleman home.

### The killings

On May 5, 2009, police found 31-year-old Sheri Coleman and her sons, 11-year-old Garett and 9-year-old Gavin, dead in their home in Columbia, a small city across the Mississippi River from St. Louis. Investigators said all three had been strangled.

The discovery followed a 911 call from Christopher Coleman, who claimed he was worried after being unable to reach his family while he was away at a gym. But investigators soon began focusing on Coleman himself.

Authorities said threatening messages had been sent before the murders, including threats that appeared to target Coleman’s family because of his job with Joyce Meyer Ministries, a prominent Christian organization based in the St. Louis area. Coleman worked as a security official for the ministry and had been involved in protecting Joyce Meyer and her family.

Prosecutors later argued those threats were staged by Coleman to create the appearance that someone else had a motive to harm his family.

### Criminal conviction

Christopher Coleman was charged with murdering Sheri, Garett and Gavin. At trial, prosecutors presented evidence that Coleman was leading a double life and wanted to escape his marriage. They argued he killed his wife and children so he could pursue a relationship with another woman while preserving his job and public image.

In 2011, a jury convicted Coleman of three counts of first-degree murder. He was sentenced to life in prison without the possibility of parole.

The criminal verdict did not end the legal fallout.

### The wrongful death lawsuit

A wrongful death suit was filed in Monroe County on behalf of the estates of Sheri Coleman and her sons. Joyce Meyer Ministries was named as a defendant, along with other parties connected to the case.

The suit alleged that the ministry had knowledge of threats involving Coleman and his family before the murders and failed to take adequate steps to protect Sheri, Garett and Gavin. The plaintiffs contended that because Coleman’s role at the ministry was tied to security and because the threats appeared connected to his employment, the organization had a duty to respond more forcefully.

The allegations centered on whether the ministry should have done more after threatening communications surfaced, including notifying law enforcement more urgently, warning Sheri directly, or taking other steps to safeguard the family.

Joyce Meyer Ministries denied wrongdoing. The ministry maintained that Christopher Coleman alone was responsible for the deaths and that the organization could not have predicted he would murder his own family.

### Key issue: duty to protect

At the heart of the civil case was a difficult legal question: did Joyce Meyer Ministries owe a duty of care to Sheri Coleman and her children?

Wrongful death cases often hinge on whether a defendant had a legal obligation to act and whether a failure to act contributed to the deaths. In this case, plaintiffs argued the ministry was aware of threats and had a responsibility to respond appropriately because those threats appeared tied to Coleman’s employment.

The defense position was that the ministry did not create the danger and could not reasonably foresee that its own employee was fabricating threats as part of a murder plot.

That distinction mattered. Civil liability is not the same as moral outrage. To prevail, plaintiffs needed to show more than tragedy; they needed to show that the ministry’s actions or omissions met the legal standard for negligence and that those failures were connected to the deaths.

### The role of the staged threats

The threatening messages were a central feature in both the criminal and civil proceedings.

Investigators concluded Coleman authored the threats himself, attempting to make it appear that an outside enemy of Joyce Meyer Ministries was targeting his family. Prosecutors used that evidence to support their theory that Coleman planned the murders in advance.

For the wrongful death plaintiffs, the threats were important for a different reason. They argued that even if Coleman created the threats, the ministry and others treated them as real before the murders — and therefore should have taken them seriously enough to protect the victims.

For the defense, that same fact cut the other way. If Coleman was the source of the threats, and if he was intentionally deceiving those around him, the ministry argued it could not be held responsible for failing to uncover his plan.

### Joyce Meyer Ministries’ public position

Joyce Meyer Ministries, an international Christian organization founded by televangelist Joyce Meyer, publicly expressed grief over the killings. The ministry also distanced itself from Coleman’s crimes, emphasizing that he acted personally and criminally, not on behalf of the organization.

The organization faced scrutiny because Coleman had been part of its security operation. The murders prompted questions about internal protocols, how threats were assessed, and whether Coleman’s access to ministry resources or security procedures played any role in delaying suspicion.

Still, in the criminal case, prosecutors portrayed Coleman’s employment less as an institutional failure and more as part of his attempted cover story.

### Families seek accountability

For relatives of Sheri, Garett and Gavin, the civil suit represented an effort to obtain accountability beyond Coleman’s imprisonment.

Wrongful death suits cannot bring victims back, and they do not impose criminal punishment. They can, however, force institutions to answer questions under oath, produce internal records, and potentially pay damages if negligence is proven.

The lawsuit reflected the family’s contention that Sheri and her sons were failed by people and systems that had reason to know they might be in danger.

### A case defined by betrayal

The Coleman murders remain one of the most disturbing family homicide cases in the St. Louis region’s recent history. Christopher Coleman was not an unknown intruder. He was a husband, father and security professional — someone whose job involved assessing risk and protecting others.

That fact made the wrongful death allegations especially painful. The same man entrusted with protecting a high-profile ministry was convicted of killing his own family after staging threats that appeared to come from outside.

The civil litigation in Monroe County underscored the broader question left behind by the case: when warning signs appear before a tragedy, who is responsible for recognizing them — and what must they do?

For Sheri Coleman’s family, the lawsuit was about more than damages. It was about whether the deaths of Sheri, Garett and Gavin could have been prevented.
